title: Passing the Pact: Comparing Common Ground Building and Audience Design In Multiparty Human and Human-Agent Collaborative Communication
venue: Proceedings of the 26th ACM International Conference on Intelligent Virtual Agents
one_sentence: Abstract-level evidence from a multiparty Tangram task suggests that people reuse prior conceptual pacts with less-knowledgeable human and agent addressees, while tailoring elaboration more strongly to human knowledge differences.
problem: How do conceptual-pact reuse and audience design differ when a speaker addresses human versus agent interlocutors with different knowledge in multiparty collaborative communication?
method: The accessible abstract reports a Tangram-based multiparty referential-communication comparison of human-human and human-agent dialogue under varying interlocutor knowledge. Sample size, trial sequence, agent implementation, coding reliability, and statistical model were not available.
findings: The abstract reports reuse of previously negotiated pacts when addressing less-knowledgeable human and agent partners.
It also reports greater sensitivity to knowledge differences and more elaboration in human-human than human-agent communication.
real_contribution: Directly separates surface pact reuse from partner-knowledge-sensitive audience design in a human-agent comparison, making it a close diagnostic neighbor for AMSC rather than evidence that a mutual human-agent convention has formed.
biggest_weakness: Only an abstract was accessible, so similarity cannot be interpreted as equivalence and the evidence cannot establish mutual belief, agent-side learning, shared-history causality, repair, or transfer.
claim_boundary: Supports a provisional speaker-behavior pattern in one multiparty reference task; it does not show that agents acquire, acknowledge, maintain, or repair conceptual pacts.
why_researcher_should_care: It shows that pact-term reuse and epistemically appropriate audience design must be measured separately, and it adds interlocutor knowledge and capability beliefs to the controls required by the highest-priority AMSC study.
